measurement.happened:
This week in Iran was defined by an active, escalating war with the United States, punctuated by a brief diplomatic window that failed to produce results, and by a growing domestic crisis of energy and public confidence.

ACTIVE COMBAT AND ESCALATION: The central story is that the US-Iran war, which had been in a roughly two-month lull, reignited mid-week. On November 15, Iran struck a US military base in Bahrain with six drones, killing six US service members. On November 17, the US retaliated by striking an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran then widened its Gulf attacks, hitting targets in Kuwait and striking Bahrain a second time, with an industrial facility set on fire. A third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East on November 16. The US Navy chief admitted the war is straining maritime forces, and a whistleblower soldier filed a complaint over the deadly Iranian strike. The war's cost to the US has passed 48 billion dollars. Iran struck three tankers and showed off missile launchers on November 21. The US also hit key Iranian infrastructure, though it denied being behind tech outages. Trump said Iran is developing bioweapons and that the US is looking into a dirty-bomb plan. Iran threatened to strike civilian sites if the US does the same. (Headlines: Reuters 11-15, 11-16, 11-17, 11-18, 11-21; AP 11-17, 11-18; CNN 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; BBC 11-15, 11-18; FT 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-18; TV5Monde 11-17, 11-18; Bloomberg 11-18, 11-19; WSJ 11-15, 11-17.)

DIRTY BOMB AND DC PLOT: A major intelligence story broke on November 16-17: US intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans to potentially detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, DC. Trump said the US takes it very seriously and that Iran would pay a major price if it carried it out. Secretary Rubio said there is no imminent threat to Washington. Iran dismissed the CNN report as propaganda. Trump also said Iran is looking at gas and bioweapons but downplayed the threat. This story dominated US political discussion for the rest of the week. (Headlines: CNN 11-16 through 11-18; Bloomberg 11-17; Al Jazeera 11-17; TV5Monde 11-17; BBC 11-17; CNBC 11-17; Reuters 11-17.)

HORMUZ AND MARITIME TENSION: The Strait of Hormuz was the economic battleground. Iran struck tankers, laid mines, and tightened its grip on shipping. The UK maritime agency reported two tanker incidents near Oman. Iran said a vessel hit a mine east of Hormuz. The US widened its blockade with curbs on oil transfers at sea, targeting ship-to-ship transfers. The UAE is shuttling oil past Iran in a risky operation. Oil prices fell for a third consecutive week as ample supply countered Iran risk, but the IEA warned the war could permanently slash reliance on Hormuz and that an energy-security response could cut global oil demand by 4% by 2035. Without Iranian oil, China's small refiners face pain but not collapse. (Headlines: Reuters 11-19, 11-20, 11-21; AP 11-21; Bloomberg 11-19, 11-20; WSJ 11-21; FT 11-21; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-20, 11-21; CNBC 11-21; TV5Monde 11-17; BBC 11-21.)

DIPLOMACY AND TALKS: Despite the fighting, diplomacy continued in parallel. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on November 21 for talks. Iran's foreign minister Araqchi said Iran wants diplomacy to end the war, but Trump said the terms are unacceptable. Trump said there is no rush on an Iran decision and he looks to next year. He said he wants a permanent deal to stop Iran getting nuclear weapons. Pakistan vowed to proceed with US-Iran diplomacy. Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchanged fire. The West pressed Iran at the IAEA to let inspections resume at bombed nuclear sites. The US, China, and Russia clashed over the nuclear stalemate. (Headlines: Reuters 11-20, 11-21; AP 11-20; Bloomberg 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-21; FT 11-20; WSJ 11-16; TV5Monde 11-15; Reuters 11-19.)

IRAQ AND PRO-IRAN MILITIAS: Iraq's government moved to crack down on Iran-backed militias. Iraqi security forces deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, the stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, after reaching a compromise with the group. The Iraqi leader's planned crackdown was described as his riskiest move yet. A top IRGC commander visited Iraq for talks. An Iran-backed group warned Iraqi forces against entering its stronghold. The militia rakes in hundreds of millions through oil smuggling. (Headlines: Reuters 11-19, 11-20; AP 11-17, 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-16, 11-20; TV5Monde 11-17; Reuters 11-16.)

SANCTIONS AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE: The US Treasury sanctioned Iranian trustees collecting oil revenues and a Hezbollah-linked charity. The US pressed Singapore and Malaysia on sanctions compliance. The US tightened its blockade with curbs on oil transfers at sea. Iranian oil leverage is weakening, which could push Tehran toward escalation. The US-Iran deal uncertainty weighed on the rupee and bonds. (Headlines: Reuters 11-18, 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-18, 11-19, 11-20; Bloomberg 11-19; Reuters 11-16.)

DOMESTIC IRAN: Iranian leaders fretted over public mood as gas shortages added to the war's ills. Iran will ration electricity despite its vast gas and oil reserves. A protest broke out in a southwestern town after a road crash killed 13 refinery workers. Iranian women are reclaiming their freedom to dress as they please. More educated young Iranians no longer see their future at home. Bloomberg ran a piece titled The Iranian Revolution Hiding in Plain Sight, suggesting internal transformation. A graphic memoir documented a woman's life under protests and war. (Headlines: Reuters 11-16, 11-19; TV5Monde 11-21; DW 11-21, 11-16; Bloomberg 11-20; AP 11-19.)

US DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE WAR: Congress struggled to avert a US shutdown as the Iran war divided lawmakers. Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic resolution to limit Trump's war powers. Trump defended the war in his Veterans Day address and said it played a role in the midterms. VP Vance declined to say he would have ordered Iran strikes, and Trump initially appeared angry before defending their friendship. The war cost surpassed 48 billion dollars, with lawmakers demanding unreleased estimates on base damage. (Headlines: Reuters 11-20; AP 11-19, 11-20; CNN 11-20; Bloomberg 11-20; WSJ 11-20; FT 11-20; DW 11-20; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

ASSASSINATION PLOTS AND ESPIONAGE: North Macedonia and Greece uncovered an Iran-linked assassination plot. A Pakistani man was sentenced to over 27 years in a US prison for an assassination plot targeting Trump that he said was steered from Iran. An Iranian operative accused of directing a failed terror plot at a US base declared innocence. Two men will stand trial in the UK next year over an RAF Fairford incident allegedly linked to Iran. (Headlines: Reuters 11-17, 11-18; AP 11-17, 11-18; BBC 11-18; CNN 11-18, 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

ISRAEL'S ROLE: Israel's spy chief lobbied for joint Iran strikes during a US visit. Israel urged renewed Iran strikes. Israel pivoted to cheaper air defense as Iran tensions rose. Mideast nations ramped up efforts to avert all-out war while Israel pushed for strikes. (Headlines: Reuters 11-18; AP 11-19; Bloomberg 11-20; WSJ 11-19; Al Jazeera 11-19.)

BAHRAIN AND GULF ALLIES: Bahrain intercepted multiple Iranian aerial attacks, with the IRGC claiming it targeted a US radar. Scores of Bahraini Shia clerics were given life sentences, accused of plotting with Iran. Kuwait repelled Iranian attacks. Gulf countries were under fire after the US hit Qeshm. The UAE is conducting risky Hormuz operations. (Headlines: Reuters 11-15, 11-16, 11-17, 11-21; BBC 11-15, 11-18; FT 11-16, 11-18; Al Jazeera 11-17, 11-18; TV5Monde 11-15, 11-17, 11-18; WSJ 11-21.)
measurement.expected:
MILITARY ESCALATION AND HORMUZ (almost certain): Expect continued tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran over the coming week. Iran will likely hit more tankers or shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and the US will respond with strikes on Iranian coastal or missile infrastructure. The third carrier group is in position, and Trump is considering new strikes as the military warns of strain. The pattern of the past week (Iran hits Bahrain/Kuwait, US hits Qeshm) will likely repeat. Oil prices will remain volatile, with the IEA's warning about permanently reduced Hormuz reliance keeping a floor under prices. The US blockade on oil transfers will tighten further.

DIPLOMATIC STALL AND QATARI MEDIATION (probable): The Qatari delegation's visit to Tehran on November 21 suggests a genuine attempt to keep a channel open, but Trump's insistence that terms are unacceptable and his statement that he looks to next year mean a breakthrough deal is unlikely this week. Expect more back-channel talks, possibly with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia involved, but no signed agreement. The IAEA inspection issue at bombed nuclear sites will remain a sticking point, with the US, China, and Russia continuing to clash over the nuclear stalemate.

DIRTY BOMB TENSION AND US DOMESTIC POLITICS (probable): The dirty-bomb story will continue to drive US political discourse. Expect Trump to use it as leverage in negotiations and in his public rhetoric. The US shutdown fight will be entangled with the Iran war, and Senate Republicans will likely continue blocking war-powers resolutions. Vance's public role and his relationship with Trump over the war will remain a source of friction and headlines. The 48-billion-dollar cost will be a growing political liability for both parties.

IRAQ MILITIA STANDOFF (probable): The Iraqi deployment to Jurf al-Sakhar and the compromise with Kataib Hezbollah will be tested. Expect at least one skirmish or standoff between Iraqi forces and the militia in the coming days. The IRGC will try to mediate from behind the scenes. The militia's oil-smuggling revenue stream will be under pressure. This is Iraq's riskiest move yet, and the coming week will reveal whether the compromise holds.

DOMESTIC IRAN: ENERGY CRISIS AND PUBLIC MOOD (probable): Iran's electricity rationing and gas shortages will worsen as the war grinds on. Expect more protests, particularly in industrial and refinery areas, as the 13-worker bus-crash protest in the southwest signals growing frustration. The educated youth brain drain will continue to be a talking point. The women's freedom-to-dress movement will gain visibility. Bloomberg's piece on a revolution hiding in plain sight suggests internal political shifts are underway, but a full-scale uprising is not expected this week.

NUCLEAR PROGRAM AND IAEA (possible): The West will press harder at the IAEA for inspections at bombed sites. Iran will likely resist or negotiate access in a limited way. The question of whether Iran could reverse its civil-only nuclear policy will be debated, but no major announcement is expected this week. The US, China, and Russia will continue to clash over the framework.

YEMEN AND HOUTHI FRONT (possible): The Saudi-Houthi exchange of fire and the anti-Houthi retreat in Yemen suggest the southern front is active. Expect more Houthi attacks on shipping or Saudi targets, with Iran backing them. This will add another dimension to the Gulf escalation.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES: A major Iranian strike on a US carrier or a large US strike on Tehran's capital (possible but not the base case). A sudden US-Iran ceasefire announcement mediated by Qatar (unlikely given Trump's tone). A second dirty-bomb or chemical-weapon scare in a US city (possible if intelligence leaks continue). A large-scale protest or uprising in Tehran triggered by the energy crisis (possible but would require a specific trigger event). A US Congressional vote to end the war (unlikely while Republicans hold the Senate). An Israeli ground or major air operation into Iran (possible but Israel would need US buy-in, which Trump is not yet giving).

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full-scale US ground invasion of Iran. A formal declaration of war by either side. Iran detonating a dirty bomb in DC within this exact week (the intelligence says planning, not execution). A complete collapse of the Iranian government or a leadership change. A US-Iran permanent deal signed before Thanksgiving. A major earthquake or natural disaster in Iran. A full internet shutdown in Iran (they have been managing with partial throttling rather than total blackout). A US Navy mutiny or mass resignation over the war's toll.
emoji_reasons: The dominant story of the week is active, escalating war between the US and Iran, with strikes on Qeshm, Bahrain, and Kuwait, three US carriers deployed, and the war cost passing 48 billion dollars.

The Strait of Hormuz was the economic and military flashpoint, with tankers hit by mines, the US tightening its oil-transfer blockade, and the IEA warning the war could permanently reshape global energy flows.

Despite the fighting, diplomacy never fully stopped: Qatar mediated in Tehran, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia pushed talks, the IAEA pressed on inspections, and Trump and Araqchi kept trading public signals that a deal remains possible even as terms are called unacceptable.

delta.motion: The most dramatic change between the two photographs is the speed and intensity of military escalation. In the first photograph, the war was described as a grinding, low-intensity confrontation with periodic spikes, with Trump declaring it 'effectively over' and both sides calibrating carefully. In the second photograph, that careful calibration has broken down. Iran struck a US base in Bahrain and killed six service members, the US retaliated on Qeshm Island, Iran widened its attacks to Kuwait and hit Bahrain a second time, a third US carrier arrived, and the US hit key Iranian infrastructure. The war went from a status-quo standoff to an active, tit-for-tat exchange with real casualties on both sides in roughly a week. The Strait of Hormuz remained the economic battleground throughout both weeks, but the intensity stepped up: from four or five tankers hit and a naval blockade ordered, to three more tankers struck, additional mine-laying, and the US widening the blockade with curbs on ship-to-ship oil transfers. The nuclear file shrank in prominence relative to active combat. In the first photograph it was a major standalone thread with IAEA reports, the $20 million bounty, and Iran's refusal of inspections. In the second photograph it is still there but has been pushed to the side by the fighting; the IAEA is pressing for inspections at bombed nuclear sites, and the US, China, and Russia are clashing over the stalemate, but no dramatic nuclear event occurred. The France cyberattack (the supermarket fridge hack) that was a genuinely new and unusual story in the first photograph has largely vanished from the second week's headlines, replaced by a broader pattern of espionage and assassination plots in Europe and the Gulf. A new and major thread appeared in the second photograph that was absent in the first: the dirty bomb and Washington DC plot, which dominated US political discussion for several days. Iraq and the pro-Iran militias also emerged as a distinct, prominent story in the second photograph, with the Iraqi government moving to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah in Jurf al-Sakhar, a move described as the Iraqi leader's riskiest yet. This thread was barely present in the first photograph. The domestic Iranian thread grew in visibility: from warnings about winter gas shortages and a women's training camp to actual electricity rationing, a protest in a southwestern town after a road crash killed thirteen refinery workers, and a Bloomberg piece suggesting a quiet internal transformation. The US domestic political thread grew in intensity: from the new Democratic Congress organizing and an impeachment push on Hegseth to Congress actively struggling to avert a shutdown, Senate Republicans blocking a Democratic war-powers resolution, and the war's $48 billion cost becoming a specific, contested number. The diplomatic thread shrank in ambition: from multiple parallel tracks (Vance to Pakistan, G7 in Paris, Qatari and Egyptian shuttle) to a Qatari delegation visiting Tehran and Pakistan vowing to proceed, with Trump saying there is 'no rush' and he looks to next year. The thread of smaller human stories (Nobel memoir, women's dress freedom, exiled journalists) persisted but did not grow. The thread of Israel's role grew: from a background presence to the spy chief lobbying for joint strikes and Israel urging renewed Iran strikes. The thread of Gulf allies as targets grew: Bahrain went from a single radar-site incident to multiple Iranian aerial attacks, scores of Shia clerics sentenced, and Kuwait repelling attacks. The thread of oil prices moved in an unexpected direction: from volatility and a ten-week-low-then-rebound pattern to three consecutive weeks of falling prices as ample supply countered Iran risk, a shift the IEA framed as a potential permanent structural change in global energy flows.
delta.wind: On the war escalation question, the expectation was that the status quo of low-intensity confrontation would persist, with a 25 to 30 percent chance of a significant new US campaign. The reality was more intense than the base case but less than a single decisive campaign: the war reignited with active strikes and casualties, but it remained a tit-for-tat exchange rather than a full-scale new operation. The expectation was directionally correct that escalation was possible, but the speed and the human cost (six US service members killed) exceeded the 'periodic spikes' framing. The 15 to 20 percent chance of a formal ceasefire or peace agreement did not materialize, as expected. On Hormuz, the expectation of at least one or two more tanker incidents was met and exceeded, with three tankers struck and additional mine incidents. The expectation that oil prices would stay volatile in the $85 to $100 range was wrong on direction: oil fell for a third consecutive week, which the IEA attributed to a potential permanent shift away from Hormuz reliance. The 20 percent chance of full closure did not happen, and the 10 to 15 percent chance of sudden reopening also did not happen, so the 'tension but no extreme' read was correct. The nuclear file expectation of a frozen status quo with no major event was largely correct; the IAEA pushed for inspections and the US-China-Russia clash added friction, but no test, deal, or dramatic announcement occurred. The 15 to 20 percent chance of a dramatic Iranian nuclear announcement did not materialize. On the cyber dimension, the expectation was that France or another European state would announce a retaliatory measure and that Iran might strike back. The France fridge hack story faded from the headlines, and no new major cyber operation dominated the second week. This was a miss: the cyber thread that was so prominent in the first photograph did not expand as predicted. On US domestic politics, the expectation that the Iran war would become a top legislative issue was correct and then some: Congress struggled over shutdown, the war-powers resolution was blocked, and the $48 billion cost became a specific political weapon. The 20 to 25 percent chance of a formal vote to end or limit the war was close to materializing (the resolution was introduced and blocked). The expectation of a shutdown or near-shutdown was also close, as Congress actively struggled to avert one. On Iran's domestic situation, the expectation of growing economic pressure (gas, heating, food) was correct: gas shortages, electricity rationing, and a protest in a southwestern town all appeared. The 15 to 20 percent chance of a major protest was partially met with a smaller, localized protest. The expectation of 'quiet, grinding adjustments' was broadly correct. On diplomacy, the expectation of continued back-channel activity without a signed deal was spot on: the Qatari delegation visited Tehran, Pakistan remained involved, and Trump said there was 'no rush.' The expectation that the diplomatic window was being squeezed from both sides was also correct. On the surprises list, the Israeli strike did not happen as a full surprise operation, though Israel lobbied for it. The major Iranian cyberattack on US infrastructure did not appear. The UN Security Council emergency session did not happen. The sudden nuclear posture change did not happen. The limited Hormuz transit corridor agreement did not appear. So none of the five listed surprises fully materialized, though the dirty bomb story was a surprise that was not on the list at all. On the 'things I would not bet on' list, all six held: no ground invasion, no formal state of war or total Hormuz closure, no nuclear deal, no leadership fall, no signed ceasefire, and no full-fanfare missile or nuclear test (though Iran did show off missile launchers). The biggest overall miss was underestimating the speed of re-escalation and the human cost of the strikes. The second biggest miss was the oil price direction, which fell rather than stayed volatile. The third miss was the cyber thread failing to expand as expected. The expectations were structurally sound on the broad themes (war continues, Hormuz stays tense, nuclear stays frozen, diplomacy stalls, US politics constrains) but were too calm on the intensity of the military escalation and too specific on the cyber and oil-price trajectories. The dirty bomb story, the Iraq militia crackdown, and the $48 billion cost as a specific political number all came from directions the expectations did not fully anticipate.
delta.driver: The force pushing Iran from the first photograph to the second is the collision between two domestic political clocks that neither side can pause. In Washington, the new Democratic Congress has turned the war from a foreign policy problem into a budget and war-powers fight, and the $48 billion price tag gives Democrats a concrete number to wield in a shutdown battle, forcing the Trump administration to either show it is winning (more strikes, more pressure) or find a way to declare victory without a deal. In Tehran, the tightening of sanctions on oil trustees, the expanded blockade on ship-to-ship transfers, and the visible weakening of Iran's oil leverage are squeezing the regime's fiscal room to absorb the war's costs, pushing it to escalate on the water and in the Gulf to create new negotiating leverage before its economic position deteriorates further. The dirty bomb story and the Iraq militia crackdown are both symptoms of this same pressure: each side is trying to signal resolve and expand its options while the other side is trying to make the status quo more expensive. The fundamental driver is that neither side has a clean off-ramp. Trump cannot look like he is caving after the midterms, and the IRGC cannot look like it is giving up its Hormuz card after two months of fighting. The war is being fought as much over who blinks first in domestic politics as over the geography of the Gulf, and that is what turned a 'grinding, low-intensity' standoff into an active exchange with bodies on the ground in a single week.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: Iran is in an active, escalating war with the US. The tit-for-tat has real casualties (six US service members killed in Bahrain), a third carrier is in the Gulf, Iran has widened attacks to Kuwait, and the dirty-bomb-in-DC story has injected a new layer of US political urgency. Diplomacy is alive but narrow: Qatar just visited Tehran, Pakistan is still in the loop, and Trump says there is no rush. The economic squeeze on Iran is tightening: sanctions on oil trustees, a widened blockade on ship-to-ship transfers, gas shortages, electricity rationing. Iraq is moving to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah, which is a new and risky front. The US Congress is struggling over a shutdown and a blocked war-powers resolution, with the $48 billion cost becoming a specific political weapon.

Extending each theme along its motion: The military escalation went from 'grinding low-intensity' to active strikes with bodies in one week. The natural extension is another round or two of tit-for-tat exchanges, possibly with a new target (a Gulf port, a refinery, or a second strike on a carrier group). Iran showing off missile launchers and threatening civilian sites signals it is preparing for the next escalation step. The US third carrier and the dirty-bomb story give Washington both the means and the political cover to hit harder. But Trump's 'no rush' and the Qatari visit suggest he is not ready for a full-scale new campaign this week. So I expect continued active exchanges, possibly one new significant strike on each side, but not a decisive new operation.

Hormuz: the motion shows intensity stepping up (three tankers, mines, widened blockade). The natural extension is one or two more tanker incidents, possibly a mine strike, and continued US naval operations. But the wind tells me I have been wrong on oil price direction (they fell three weeks running despite the war). So I should not expect a dramatic price spike even if a tanker is hit. The IEA's structural-shift warning suggests markets are decoupling from Hormuz risk faster than I assumed.

Diplomacy: the motion shows it shrinking in ambition. Qatar just visited, Trump says no rush, Pakistan is still involved. The natural extension is continued back-channel activity, possibly another phone call or a second Qatari visit, but no signed deal. The dirty-bomb story complicates things by giving the US a reason to be more hawkish, but Rubio's 'no imminent threat' suggests it is more political than operational. I expect diplomacy to continue but remain stalled, with both sides using the talks as cover to avoid looking weak domestically.

The dirty-bomb story: this is new and dominated US politics. The natural extension is continued political debate, possibly new intelligence details, Iran's dismissal or counter-claim, and the story being used as justification for a new sanctions package or a more aggressive posture. But I do not expect the bomb to actually be detonated or for a US security operation to be launched this week. It is a political weapon, not an operational plan.

Iraq: the crackdown on Kataib Hezbollah in Jurf al-Sakhar is new and described as the Iraqi leader's riskiest move. The natural extension is the Iraqi government proceeding with the operation, possibly with some friction or a pause. The IRGC commander's visit suggests Iran is trying to manage the situation. I expect the crackdown to proceed but with some compromise, and possibly a minor clash or exchange of fire. If it goes badly, it could trigger a new Iranian response, but a full militia war seems unlikely this week.

Domestic Iran: gas shortages and electricity rationing will continue into winter. The motion shows growing visibility (protest in SW town, Bloomberg 'quiet revolution' piece). The natural extension is continued economic pressure, possibly another localized protest, and continued social change (women's dress, youth emigration). I do not expect a major nationwide protest wave, but the grinding pressure is building.

US domestic politics: the shutdown threat is active, the war-powers resolution was blocked, the $48 billion cost is a political weapon. The natural extension is continued Congressional friction, possibly another vote or near-vote, and the dirty-bomb story keeping the war in the spotlight. I expect the shutdown to be averted (barely) but the war to remain a contested issue.

Correcting for the wind: I have been underestimating the speed of military escalation and the human cost. So I should expect slightly more active combat than a 'status quo' read. I have been getting oil prices wrong (they fell, not stayed volatile). So I should be more cautious on price direction and expect continued volatility with a slight downward bias. I have been overestimating the cyber thread. So I should lower the probability of a major new cyber operation. I have been underestimating domestic political shocks on both sides. So I should expect at least one new Congressional action or a visible political rupture. The dirty-bomb story and the Iraq crackdown are new variables that shift the probability distribution toward more active events.

The less-likely surprises the motion makes more likely: (1) A new Iranian strike on a major Gulf city or a second hit on a US carrier group, because Iran is showing off launchers and threatening civilian sites. (2) A US strike on a major Iranian oil or gas facility, because the dirty-bomb story gives political cover for a harder hit. (3) A visible US security operation or intelligence briefing in DC related to the dirty-bomb plot, because the story has dominated politics and Trump said Iran would 'pay a major price.' (4) A minor clash in Jurf al-Sakhar during the Iraqi crackdown, because the operation is described as risky and the militia warned against entry. (5) A new sanctions package targeting Iranian oil revenue channels, because the US is pressing Singapore and Malaysia and the oil-leverage-weakening narrative is driving policy.

What I would not bet on: a full-scale US ground invasion, a formal declaration of war, total closure of Hormuz, a signed ceasefire or peace deal, a change in Iran's leadership, a nuclear test or NPT withdrawal, the dirty bomb actually being detonated, a major Iranian cyberattack on US power infrastructure, or a joint US-Israeli ground operation. All of these remain possible but the motion and the domestic political constraints on both sides make them less likely than the active-but-managed escalation I am forecasting.

(2) A visible US intelligence or security operation in DC related to the dirty-bomb plot, with a public briefing or a new arrest. (3) A new Iranian drone or missile strike on a Gulf capital (Dubai, Doha, or Riyadh) as a test of the civilian-site threat. (4) A minor but dramatic clash in Jurf al-Sakhar, with casualties on the Iraqi side, forcing a pause in the crackdown. (5) A new sanctions package targeting a major Iranian oil-revenue channel, possibly a Chinese or Indian bank, as the US tightens the economic squeeze.

What I would not bet on this week: a full-scale US ground invasion of Iran; a formal declaration of war by either side; total closure of the Strait of Hormuz; a signed ceasefire or peace agreement; a change in Iran's supreme leadership; a nuclear test or NPT withdrawal; the dirty bomb actually being detonated in Washington; a major Iranian cyberattack on US power-grid infrastructure; or a joint US-Israeli ground operation. All remain possible but the domestic political constraints on both sides and the active-but-managed tempo of the war make them less likely than the continued tit-for-tat I am forecasting.
crystal.headline: Iran Strikes Gulf Again as Dirty Bomb Fears Grip Washington
emoji_reasons: Active tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, with new attacks on Gulf targets and Iranian infrastructure, define the week's central drama.
The Strait of Hormuz remains the economic battleground, with tanker strikes, mine-laying, and a widening US naval blockade shaping global oil flows.
US domestic politics, from the shutdown fight to the dirty-bomb debate and the $48 billion war cost, constrain and amplify every military and diplomatic decision.
crystal.tldr: Expect another round of US-Iran strikes, with Iran hitting a Gulf target and the US responding on Iranian soil, possibly a new oil or military site. The dirty-bomb-in-DC story will dominate US politics and give Washington cover for a harder posture, while diplomacy through Qatar and Pakistan continues but produces no deal. Oil prices stay volatile with a slight downward bias, and Iraq's risky crackdown on Kataib Hezbollah adds a new front.
crystal.eli5:
Imagine two neighbors who are in a big argument and keep throwing things over the fence. Last week, one neighbor (Iran) threw a rock and hit the other one (the US) in the face. This week, they are still throwing things. Iran is probably going to throw another rock at a friend of the US neighbor (one of the Gulf countries), and the US neighbor is going to throw a bigger rock back at Iran, maybe at a place where they make oil or keep their missiles. They are also talking to each other through a mutual friend (Qatar), but nobody is ready to shake hands and say the argument is over.

There is also a scary story going around that Iran might try to make a dirty bomb in Washington, the US capital. It probably will not actually happen, but it is making everyone in Washington very nervous and angry. The president is using it as a reason to be tougher, and the people in Congress are arguing about whether the president should be allowed to keep fighting. They are also arguing about who pays for all the fighting, because it has already cost about 48 billion dollars, which is a lot of money.

In the water between Iran and the rest of the world (the Strait of Hormuz), ships are still getting hit by mines or drones. This is important because a lot of the world's oil goes through that water. But strangely, oil prices are going down a little, not up, because the world is slowly learning to find other ways to get oil. In Iraq, the government is trying to kick out a group of fighters who work for Iran, and that could get messy. At home in Iran, people are running out of gas for heating and electricity is being cut, and some people are getting angry, but not enough to cause a huge revolution just yet.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A's central assumption was that the war was in a 'grinding, unresolved state' of low-intensity confrontation that would persist. In reality, the war had been in a roughly two-month lull that broke mid-week, with Iran striking a US base in Bahrain (killing six service members), the US retaliating on Qeshm Island, and Iran widening attacks to Kuwait. A misread the baseline: the 'status quo' was a lull, not a grinding stalemate, and it broke. That said, A's 25-to-30 percent probability for 'a significant new US air or missile campaign' landed close to what happened (the Qeshm strike and hits on Iranian infrastructure). A correctly called the absence of a formal ceasefire or deal, the Hormuz tanker and mine incidents (though it expected one or two, and there were more), the nuclear freeze, the continuation of multi-track diplomacy (Qatar, Pakistan, Egypt), and the rise of US domestic politics around the war (Senate blocking a resolution, shutdown struggle, Trump's Veterans Day defense). A's domestic Iran section (gas shortages, women's stories, economic pressure) matched the week well. A's cyber section focused heavily on the France-fridge-hack follow-through, which was less prominent than expected; the actual espionage stories (North Macedonia/Greece assassination plot, UK RAF Fairford trial, Pakistani man's 27-year sentence) were broader and more varied. A's 'less likely surprises' list included a surprise Israeli strike (which materialized as the spy chief lobbying for strikes) and a major Iranian cyberattack on US infrastructure (the dirty bomb plot in DC was a different but related 'unconventional threat to the US' story that A at least gestured toward). A missed the Iraq militia crackdown entirely, the whistleblower complaint, the $48 billion cost becoming a headline, the third carrier's arrival, the US Navy's use of expired Tomahawks, and the Bahraini Shia clerics' life sentences. A's oil price range of $85 to $100 was slightly high; oil actually fell for a third consecutive week. Overall, A captured the broad shape of the week (Hormuz tension, no deal, nuclear freeze, US politics, domestic pressure) but underestimated the escalation from lull to active combat and the specific bloodshed (six US soldiers killed, Kuwait attacks).
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B's eight themes provided a structured picture that was largely directionally correct. Theme 1 (Hormuz) predicted 'two to three' vessel incidents, which matched the actual multiple tanker strikes and mine incidents more closely than A's 'one or two.' The US naval blockade widening and the UAE's risky oil-shuttling operation both materialized. Theme 2 (US politics) correctly anticipated a major Congressional action (the Senate blocking the Democratic war-powers resolution), the shutdown risk becoming concrete, and Trump responding with a strength-showing speech (the Veterans Day address). The 'less-likely surprise' of Trump ordering a significant new strike was close to the Qeshm Island hit. Theme 3 (diplomacy) correctly called multiple parallel tracks with no signed deal, and the Qatari delegation's Tehran visit on November 21 fit this. Theme 4 (nuclear) correctly predicted the frozen, adversarial posture with IAEA pressure and no dramatic physical event. Theme 5 (cyber) focused on France crystallizing a response, which was less prominent than expected; the actual espionage and assassination-plot stories were broader and involved more countries. Theme 6 (covert/intelligence activity in Europe) was the most broadly accurate theme: the North Macedonia/Greece assassination plot, the UK RAF Fairford trial, the Pakistani man's 27-year sentence, and the Iranian operative's innocence plea all fit this pattern. Theme 7 (economic) got the gas shortage and IEA warning right, and its $80-to-$95 oil range was closer to actual than A's $85-to-$100, since oil fell for a third week. Theme 8 (domestic) correctly called the women's stories, economic pain, and the absence of a mass protest or leadership change. B missed the dirty bomb/DC plot story entirely, which dominated US political discussion for much of the week. B also missed the Iraq militia crackdown, the whistleblower complaint, the $48 billion cost headline, the third carrier, the expired Tomahawks, and the Bahraini clerics' sentences. Like A, B's framing of 'continued disruption' implied the war was already active, when it was actually in a lull that broke. B's overall picture was solid and well-organized, but the absence of the dirty bomb story and the Iraq angle are notable gaps.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts shared the same fundamental misread: they assumed the war was in an ongoing active (if low-level) state, when in fact it was in a two-month lull that broke into a more intense phase of combat. Both correctly captured the major steady-state themes: Hormuz tension with tanker and mine incidents, no formal deal, nuclear freeze, multi-track diplomacy, US political pressure on the war, domestic economic strain in Iran, and the absence of a regime-level political change. Both missed the Iraq militia crackdown, the whistleblower complaint, the $48 billion cost becoming a marquee figure, the third carrier's arrival, and the expired Tomahawks story. The key differentiator is the dirty bomb/DC plot. This was one of the dominant stories of the week, generating headlines across CNN, Bloomberg, Reuters, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde, and others. Forecast A listed a 'major Iranian cyberattack on US financial or energy infrastructure' as a less-likely surprise, which is not the same as a dirty bomb plot in Washington, but it at least flagged the category of an unconventional, high-impact Iranian threat against the US homeland. Forecast B did not mention this story in any of its eight themes or its less-likely surprises. For a reader trying to understand the week, A's inclusion of this as a watch-item is a meaningful edge. A also mentioned a surprise Israeli strike as a less-likely possibility, which materialized in the form of Israel's spy chief lobbying for joint strikes during a US visit. B's espionage theme (Theme 6) was more broadly accurate than A's France-specific cyber focus, and B's oil price range was closer to actual. B's 'two to three vessel incidents' was more accurate than A's 'one or two.' However, the dirty bomb story's absence from B, combined with A's more specific escalation probabilities (25-30 percent for a new US campaign, which was in the right range), gives A a slight edge in helping a reader anticipate the week's most surprising and politically significant development. Both forecasts would have served a reader reasonably well, but A's marginally better coverage of the week's biggest surprise and its more granular escalation probabilities tip the balance. VERDICT: A
